h.select_rule: Keep hypotheses whose direction follows almost mechanically: condition on the edited field's own current value, or on a field that cuts off the edited part's input or output. Drop hypotheses relying on cross-field redundancy or competing effects. Keep diverse edit fields.
h.strategy: Favor the most reliable kinds of conditional effects. (1) Self-conditioning: an edit's effect depends most on what it replaces, so it is more positive when the parent's current value of that field is weak, empty or harmful, and more negative when the current value is strong. (2) Disconnection: an edit matters little when the edited part receives no input or cannot reach the output under the condition. (3) Floor and ceiling: gains are larger when the parent is poor overall and smaller when it is already near the best. Use cross-field redundancy only when the redundancy is near-total. Cover many different edit fields and values. Give a one-sentence mechanism for each.

hyps.why: With edge 0 none, node 1 gets no input, so edge 2 is disconnected and the conv gain vanishes.
Edge 4 starts at node 1, which is empty when edge 0 is none, so the edit has little effect.
Replacing a removed edge with a 3x3 conv adds far more than replacing an op that already carries features.
A skip reconnects node 2 to the input, gaining more than replacing a working op.
A skip on the direct input-to-output edge adds a gradient-friendly path that is missing when the edge is none.
Edge 5 is the last hop from node 2, so filling it with a conv restores a major route to the output.
Removing a strong direct edge hurts far more than removing a weak one.
A skip adds a useful residual path where none existed.
A skip fills an empty edge with an easy-to-train path, which is worth more than replacing an existing op.
Removing a strong conv edge costs more accuracy than removing a weak op.
